newsitem.title: UK: TENNIS-SOGGY WIMBLEDON 'FARCE' SET TO CONTINUE.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-SOGGY WIMBLEDON 'FARCE' SET TO CONTINUE.

text.p: The 1997 Wimbledon championships are in increasing danger of going down in history as 'the biggest farce on grass' ever hosted by the All England Club.

As rain continued to pour down on Friday, the tournament has already assured itself of a place in the bad weather 'hall of fame' and, barring a major improvement over the weekend, looks certain to be extended into a third week.

Wimbledon officials were increasingly resigned to the prospect of a second successive day without any play on Friday, the first time two whole days have been lost since the championships were shifted to their current site in 1922.
Just 96 matches have been completed in a dismal first week, significantly fewer than in 1991 which is generally regarded as the wettest year ever.

That year, 123 matches took place in the corresponding period and tournament referee Alan Mills, forced to arrange play on the middle Sunday for the first time in history, must have thought things would never get wetter.
Sadly for Mills, the forecast remains very poor and he now faces some tough decisions.
Already it has been agreed to reduce the men's doubles from five sets to three up to the quarter-finals, and Mills admits a similar format might have to be adopted for the singles.

"It hasn't been done as far as I can remember," he said. The prospect of Sunday play is also still "being considered" but the forecast suggests it could be an academic issue. Mills himself tends towards an extension into the third week, offering the probability of a men's final on the third Monday for the first time since 1988.
For the record, here is a rundown of the limited play there has been at the championships this week.

Monday - A quarter of the scheduled programme was completed on the opening day, with rain intervening even before the first ball was struck. Second seed Goran Ivanisevic and Briton Tim Henman were among the early men's winners.
Tuesday - The only full day possible to date. World number two Michael Chang was the most notable casualty, while fellow seeds Mark Philippoussis, Gustavo Kuerten and Jonas Bjorkman also perished.
Wednesday - No play possible before 1800 local time and less than two hours in total. The only two players in the entire tournament to secure wins were Monica Seles and Jana Novotna.
Thursday - A complete wash-out, the first since 1992.
Friday - No end in sight to the rain with the prospects of play looking increasingly forlorn, although officials were delaying a final decision to abandon play until at least 1600 GMT.
For the time being, though, officials should be grateful that court coverage has improved since 1922, when the championships were first played at Church Road.
Only the Centre Court was protected by a tarpaulin, the outside courts quickly became a quagmire and the tournament was not completed until the third Wednesday.
Compared to that, Alan Mills' nightmare is only just beginning.
